frontmatter_description: Resolve which existing commitment, ongoing task, or new invitation has priority when plans conflict.
title: Commitment Priority
use_when: Use when a scene asks which plan, obligation, appointment, task, or invitation should come first.
Use when an existing commitment constrains what the character can reasonably do next.
Use when the key question is how to rank obligations, not which goal is strongest in the abstract.
do_not_use_when: Do not use when there is no prior commitment, schedule, obligation, or plan constraint.
Do not use when the main issue is general goal conflict without a commitment hierarchy.
Do not use when the question is about predicting the next action from belief and goal.
Do not use when the question is about inferring why someone acted, looked, or gestured.
Do not use when the main issue is emotion, persuasion, or social norm violation.
decision_variable: the priority order among commitments or plans
trigger_checklist: There are at least two competing items: commitment, task, invitation, appointment, or obligation.
One item is already underway, promised, scheduled, or socially binding.
The question is which item should be treated as higher priority.
The answer depends on plan constraint, not on hidden belief or emotion.
workflow: List the competing commitments or plans.
Identify which ones are already fixed by promise, schedule, deadline, or active engagement.
Rank the items by constraint strength and urgency.
Choose the option that best preserves the highest-priority commitment.

special_case.title: New invitation versus existing obligation
special_case.rule: When a new invitation conflicts with an existing promise or ongoing task, the existing commitment usually has priority unless the scene explicitly states a stronger override such as emergency, cancellation, or explicit permission to reschedule.

worked_example.scene: Maya promised to help Sam move at 3 p.m., but at 2:50 p.m. her friend invites her to lunch.
worked_example.question: What should Maya prioritize?
worked_example.answer_logic: The promised help is the prior commitment, so it outranks the new invitation.

boundary_exit_rule: Exit to micro-25 Goal-Conflict Arbitration if there is no binding commitment or schedule constraint.
Exit to micro-23 Action Prediction if the question asks what the character will do next rather than which plan has priority.
Exit to micro-22 Intention Recognition if the scene asks why the person is doing something.
Exit to micro-21 Goal Hierarchy if the issue is classifying goals as long-term versus subordinate rather than ranking commitments.
Exit to a persuasion or repair unit if the main issue is how to talk about the conflict, not which plan to honor.

references.route_signal: Use this micro unit when the scene involves competing obligations, a schedule conflict, or a choice between an existing commitment and a new request.
hard_boundary: Not for general preferences with no commitment structure.
Not for future action prediction unless the ranking of commitments is the core reason.
Not for intention reading, emotion appraisal, or norm violation by itself.
shortcut_to_avoid: Do not assume the strongest desire wins; commitment priority is not the same as preference strength.
Do not infer the next action from mood or personality when the question is about obligation order.
Do not treat any two goals as equal competitors if one is already promised or scheduled.
common_failure_modes: Confusing commitment priority with simple goal conflict.
Answering with the most enjoyable or most urgent-seeming option instead of the most binding one.
Using intention inference when the scene only asks for ranking of plans.

minimal_pair.case: The character promised to babysit at 6 p.m. and then gets a casual invitation to dinner.
minimal_pair.why_it_matches: Two plans compete, and the existing promise determines priority.

minimal_pair.case: The character wants to finish homework or play a game.
minimal_pair.why_it_matches: This is ordinary goal conflict with no commitment constraint, so it does not match.

boundary_stress_test: If the scene has only a wish and a temptation, do not use this unit.
If a promise was already canceled or explicitly made flexible, the commitment constraint may no longer decide priority.
If the question asks what someone will likely choose because of habit or emotion, this is the wrong unit unless priority ordering is explicit.
references.generalization_note: This unit generalizes across calendars, promises, deadlines, duties, invitations, and active tasks whenever the task is to rank which commitment should take precedence.

validation_seed.positive_pattern: A person has an existing promise or active task and must decide whether a new request should override it.
validation_seed.near_miss_pattern: A person has two desires with no explicit obligation or schedule.
validation_seed.boundary_pattern: A person is asked why they acted, not which plan had priority.

notes: Keep the focus on priority ordering, not on social niceness or emotional reaction.
Treat explicit promises, deadlines, and ongoing tasks as stronger evidence than casual preferences.
core_question: Resolve priority among existing commitments, ongoing tasks, and new invitations
